title: Vinyl Records: Black Magic at Work
summary: Josh and Chuck announce a return to live shows in early February (Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco during SketchFest) with ticket presale and general sale dates in October. They then explore vinyl records: the recent comeback and sales figures, the history of recorded sound from Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville's phonautograph through Edison's phonograph, Alexander Graham Bell's graphophone and wax cylinders, Emile Berliner's shellac discs and gramophone, and the 78 RPM standard and why it was chosen. Next they cover PVC vinyl's 1930s origins, Peter Goldmark's LP at 33⅓ RPM, the speed war with 45s, early stereo records, and the Beatles' stereo experiments. The hosts then explain how records are made (lacquer cutting, metal masters and stampers, pressing from PVC pellets, carbon black for dust), how a stylus reads the groove and plays back, and the analog versus digital debate including streaming bitrates. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about farting after colonoscopies and a sign-off.

segments.title: Live show announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce returning to live shows in February in Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco (SketchFest), with presale on October 6 and general sale on October 7. They introduce the episode's wax-themed title and say they will discuss vinyl.

segments.title: Vinyl sales decline and comeback
segments.summary: The hosts review vinyl sales stats: about 600 million records bought per year at the seventies peak, a drop to about 0.1 percent of sales in the nineties, a comeback in the 2000s, and vinyl outselling CDs in 2021. They also discuss DJs and vinyl use.

segments.title: Phonautograph and early sound recording
segments.summary: Scott de Martinville's phonautograph used a boar's hair stylus on a soot-covered glass plate to record sound, and recordings were later played back digitally. The hosts discuss the importance of a consistent playback speed.

segments.title: Edison, Bell, and wax cylinders
segments.summary: Edison recorded sound from a diaphragm stylus onto paraffin wax and then metal cylinders. Alexander Graham Bell changed cylinders to wax and built the graphophone. The hosts describe hand-crank players and a story about Joe Bussard's wax cylinder collection.

segments.title: Berliner, gramophone, shellac, and 78 RPM
segments.summary: Emile Berliner introduced flat disc records made of shellac, which could be mass produced from molds. The hosts explain the 78 RPM standard, derived from a motor speed of 3600 RPM stepped down by gears, and the fragility and short playing time of shellac discs.

segments.title: PVC vinyl, Goldmark LP, and the speed war
segments.summary: Vinyl (PVC) was first tried by RCA Victor in 1930 but failed. After World War II, Peter Goldmark at CBS developed the 33⅓ RPM long-play LP with finer grooves. Columbia released the LP and RCA Victor the 45 RPM single, a format war that ended with both coexisting.

segments.title: Stereo records and personal record memories
segments.summary: Stereo records were developed in the 1950s to carry two channels in one groove, with the outer wall for the right channel and the inner wall for the left. The Beatles were among early stereo experimenters. The hosts share their first records and their experience with tapes and CDs.

segments.title: How records are made: cutting, stamping, pressing
segments.summary: Records are cut on a lathe with a ruby chisel into a lacquer mother disc, which is electroplated into a metal master stamper used to press around 100,000 copies. PVC pellets with carbon black are pressed with about sixty tons of pressure, and the excess flash is recycled. Black color is chosen because carbon black reduces static and dust.

segments.title: Playback, analog vs digital, and streaming
segments.summary: A stylus reads the groove and a cartridge converts it to an electrical signal. The hosts discuss the analog versus digital debate, using a door-jamb height analogy and noting that CD quality is much higher than streaming bitrates, and that records made from digital files exist.

segments.title: Listener mail: farting after colonoscopies
segments.summary: A listener who works as a gastroenterology technician explains that air versus carbon dioxide used during colonoscopies causes different amounts of post-procedure gas.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give the contact email and network credits.
